props.title: Blow

sections.content: Blow (2001) stands as one of the defining drug trafficking films of the 2000s, with Johnny Depp delivering a nuanced portrayal of real-life cocaine smuggler George Jung. Director Ted Demme crafts a compelling rise-and-fall narrative that sits alongside classics like Goodfellas (1990) and Scarface (1983), but with a distinctly American Dream-gone-wrong perspective. The film's sun-drenched 1970s aesthetic and attention to period detail creates a vivid backdrop for Jung's transformation from small-town pot dealer to Pablo Escobar's American connection.

sections.content: The crime biopic genre evolved significantly with films like Blow, moving away from the operatic violence of earlier drug films toward more character-driven narratives. Like American Made (2017) and The Wolf of Wall Street (2013), it explores the intoxicating allure of easy money and the inevitable price of excess. Depp's Jung represents a unique antihero - not a violent kingpin like Tony Montana, but a businessman who gets in way over his head. SUBHEAD: The Rise and Fall Structure in Drug Crime Films

Blow perfected a narrative template that influenced later films like Kill the Messenger (2014) and White Boy Rick (2018). The film's structure - showing Jung's childhood, meteoric rise, and devastating fall - became a blueprint for modern crime biopics. What sets it apart is Ray Liotta's powerful performance as Jung's father, adding emotional depth rarely seen in the genre and echoing his own role in Goodfellas (1990).
